Read against the code that framing is wrong: stackvo.json needs no flow — it is already in the project directory, already schema-validated, and a teammate who clones the repo already has it. What they do NOT get is the STACK: which of the twenty services are enabled and at which versions. That lives in .env, the one file nobody commits, because it is also where every password is. So the clone succeeds, the manifest is perfect, and the project still will not start until somebody says "you need MySQL 8.0, Redis and Elasticsearch on". That sentence is the preset.
preset_export.notes: A preset can never carry a secret, and that is enforced by construction rather than by filtering. `services` entries hold `enabled` and `version` — two named fields, not a passthrough map — so there is no code path by which SERVICE_MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD reaches one; it is not that a filter drops it, it is that there is nowhere to put it. `settings` is an ALLOW-LIST of five global keys, not a deny-list: Env::is_secret matches on suffix, so a key added upstream tomorrow called SERVICE_FOO_APIKEY would sail through a deny-list. An allow-list fails closed against a file this app does not own. Disabled services are included too — a preset listing only what is on cannot express "and turn Elasticsearch off", which is half of what makes two machines match. Ports and paths are excluded on purpose: they are properties of one developer's machine, and importing somebody else's is how two people end up fighting over 3306.

preset_plan.why: Importing a colleague's stack must never be a blind write over your own. Same shape as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and cert_plan/cert_apply — the pattern this app already uses everywhere a change leaves its own process.
preset_plan.notes: Rejections are NAMED, never silently dropped: an unknown service id, or a settings key outside the allow-list, appears in `rejected` with its reason. A preset that quietly ignores half of what it was given is how somebody concludes the feature works and then spends an afternoon on the service it skipped. Unknown ids are refused here rather than becoming a SERVICE_<JUNK>_ENABLE key in the user's .env and a compose profile that matches nothing — the failure mode CONFLICTS.md C-09 records. A file that is valid JSON but not a preset (`kind` mismatch) is an error, not a plan with zero changes: pointing the importer at a package.json has to say so rather than look successful. A preset from a NEWER version is refused rather than half-read.

preset_save.notes: Pretty-printed, because the point of the file is being read in a pull request. Written atomically.

profiler_clear.why: Profiling fills a disk fast — the 200,000-iteration loop that shaped the parser produced a 10 MB file from one run — so "clear these" has to be one button, not sixty.

profiler_delete.notes: `id` is a bare `cachegrind.out.*` file name, checked before it is joined to a path — the same handle-not-a-path rule app_log_open runs on.

profiler_read.notes: Cachegrind, read off real Xdebug 3.4.0 output rather than from a specification. Four properties decide the parser. (1) Names are COMPRESSED and the ids are NOT in order — a real file defined fl=(2) before fl=(1), and cfn=(n) can reference a name defined further down, so names are resolved at the end; resolving as you read produces blanks. (2) Every call gets its own block: a 200,000-iteration loop produced **200,004 fn= blocks across 1.6 million lines**, so aggregating by name is not a nicety. (3) A cost line's meaning depends on what preceded it — after fn= it is SELF cost, after calls= it is the INCLUSIVE cost of that call, attributed to the callee. Getting that wrong doubles every caller's self time and is invisible in the output. (4) Units are declared in the file (`events: Time_(10ns) Memory_(bytes)`), not fixed — assuming microseconds would be wrong by two orders of magnitude on this build. `percent` is a share of `selfTotal`, not of the file's `summary`: that denominator is the one that makes "how much of the work happened in here" true and adds to 100. A gzipped file is REFUSED with an explanation rather than parsed into nonsense. Capped at 256 MB with `truncated` reported, because a truncated profile with no warning is a performance conclusion drawn from half the data.

profiler_set_mode.notes: Stored in `projects/<name>/.stackvo/xdebug.json`, beside php.ini and devserver.json, for the same two reasons: the manifest schema is additionalProperties:false, and a file under .stackvo/ travels with a clone. On/off stays in `php.extensions`, because that is what compiles the extension in. Switching to `profile` writes `generated/xdebug/<name>.ini` and mounts it read-only at /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/zzz-stackvo-xdebug.ini. **Why an ini and not the environment**: measured against a running container, XDEBUG_CONFIG does carry `output_dir` and `start_with_request` — both took effect — but it silently ignores `use_compression`, and Xdebug 3.4 gzips by default. One compressed file is the difference between a profile view and a parse error. `zzz-` rather than `zz-` because zz-stackvo.ini is the USER's php.ini from php_ini_set; a name sorting before it would let a hand-written xdebug.output_dir send profiles somewhere this app cannot read, which presents as profiling that produced nothing. The mode itself stays in XDEBUG_MODE and is deliberately absent from the ini: the environment variable takes precedence over xdebug.mode, so setting both invites them to disagree.

profiler_status.why: P3-17 named Blackfire and SPX, and both are the wrong door. Blackfire ships a template already and needs an ACCOUNT — a signup wall in a local development tool. SPX, XHProf and Excimer are not in contracts/php-extensions.json (only xdebug is), so adding one is a change to a contract shared with upstream, the same class of decision as the Mailpit swap. **Xdebug is already a profiler**: xdebug.mode=profile writes cachegrind files, the extension is in the catalog, and the overlay that sets XDEBUG_MODE already belongs to this app. That is the one route with no contract change attached.
profiler_status.notes: Profiling is a MODE of the existing Xdebug toggle, not a second switch — the extension has to be compiled in either way, and two switches for one extension is two states to explain instead of one. The mode is `debug` or `profile`, never both: they want opposite start triggers (stepping wants to connect on the next request, profiling wants a trigger so an idle stack does not write a multi-megabyte file per page load), so a combined mode would have to break one of them. `trigger` is the name a request must carry — XDEBUG_TRIGGER as a cookie, GET, POST or environment value.

args.name: string
args.spec: ProjectSpec (optional — defaults to what was detected)
args.overrides: { domain?, phpVersion?, server?, extensions? } — each replaces one detected value

project_adopt.why: Writes stackvo.json for a directory that is already there, then regenerates. The counterpart of project_create, which requires the directory to be absent.
project_adopt.notes: Refuses when a manifest already exists — adopting a managed project would silently overwrite settings the user chose. The spec is validated against project.schema.json exactly as project_create's is; detection fills the form, it does not bypass the check. `overrides` sit on top of detection rather than replacing it, one value at a time: detection reads the code and can say "this is Laravel, its document root is public", but it has no way to know the user wanted `shop.loc`, and the three PHP fields are the scaffolding gap — a composer.json states the version the framework NEEDS (`"php": "^8.3"`), which read as an answer pins a new Laravel to the floor of its own range, nothing in a checkout names a web server, and detection has no opinion about extensions at all, so an adopted project took the generator's seven-entry fallback. The PHP three apply only when the detected spec has a `php` block, so a Node template cannot pick up a second runtime block (W-02). Passing a full spec still bypasses detection entirely; passing overrides does not. Also writes the project's hosts entry and extends the certificate — see project_create.

project_adoptable.why: `project_create` refuses when the directory already exists, so a folder cloned into projects/ could not be brought under management at all — the only way in was writing stackvo.json by hand. On the checkout this was written against, 11 of 21 directories under projects/ were in that state: real code, unmanaged.
project_adoptable.notes: Reads only, and needs no Docker. Each entry carries a detected runtime, server, document root and framework, plus the files that detection was based on — a document root inferred wrongly produces a project that builds, starts and serves a 404, which is a failure with no error attached to it.

project_clone.returns: { operationId: OperationId, name: string, hasManifest: boolean }
project_clone.why: The only way a repository reached the workspace was the user cloning it in a terminal and then adopting the folder. The clone is the one step the app was not doing, and it is the first one.
project_clone.notes: StackVo authenticates NOTHING. No keys, no agent, no known_hosts, no tokens, no host trust — git and ssh read the user's own config, and a URL that works in their terminal works here. GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15' are set for one reason only: a windowless subprocess must fail rather than wait for an answer nobody can give. StrictHostKeyChecking is deliberately NOT disabled — silently trusting an unknown host is the one failure worth stopping for. No host is special-cased; a self-hosted forge on a company domain is the case this was built for. The URL is the first webview-supplied string in this codebase to reach a subprocess argv, so `git::parse` is an allowlist of two shapes (ssh/https URL, or scp-style user@host:path) rather than a filter: `ext::` transports execute commands, a leading `-` is read by git as an option, and file:// is not a network fetch. Emits scaffold:progress / scaffold:done deliberately — same step of the same flow, and the console already subscribes. Ends with code on disk. `hasManifest` says which follow-up the caller owes, and the two are opposites: a repository without a stackvo.json is adopted (detect, then write one), a repository with one is registered (the committed settings are the team's answer and are not overwritten). Cloning a repository that ships its manifest — the arrangement the file is commit-friendly for — used to end in "already has a stackvo.json" with nothing generated. Either way a clone never becomes a second way to create a project.

worktree_support.why: N. Everything a project can say about worktrees before a dialog opens: whether git is here, whether the directory is a repository, which branches exist and which of them are already checked out somewhere, which database instances a branch could be given a database on, and the worktrees this project already has. One call rather than five, because the answer decides whether the button is even drawn.
worktree_support.notes: `reason` is a sentence, not a boolean — 'not a git repository', 'itself a worktree', 'no domain in its manifest'. `linked` is git's own answer (a linked checkout has its own git dir and a shared common dir), which is a different question from `record`: `record` means this app made it and therefore knows what it gave it. Branches come back newest-commit-first, because the branch somebody wants a worktree for is almost always one they touched this week. Instances that are stopped are listed and marked rather than hidden: 'why is that greyed out' has an answer on the row, 'why is the list empty' does not.

worktree_list.why: Every worktree in the workspace, so the projects list can say `branch of shop` on a row instead of showing two unrelated siblings. Asking per project would be one command per row.
worktree_list.notes: Each row carries what is true right now beside what was recorded: `exists` for the directory, `dirty` for uncommitted work (null when git could not answer — the same third state `projectLocalRead` reports for ignore rules), and `orphaned` when the registration outlived the checkout. Reads two files and asks git per row; no Docker call, so it answers with the engine down.

args.name: string
args.options: { newBranch?: boolean, name?: string, database?: 'none' | 'create' | 'copy', instance?: string }?

worktree_plan.why: A worktree creates a directory, a hostname, a container and a database at once, and the only moment any of those can be argued with is before they exist. The same plan-then-apply pair as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and db_move_plan/db_move_apply.
worktree_plan.notes: No side effects — safe to call on every keystroke in the branch field. A refused plan still carries the name, path, hostname and database it *would* have produced, because a dialog that blanks out when it says no makes the reason harder to act on. `refused` is one sentence naming the cause: git missing, the project not a repository or itself one, no `domain` to build under, a branch git will not accept, a branch already checked out elsewhere (git allows one working tree per branch), a directory or hostname already taken, or a database instance that is absent or stopped. `warnings` is for what proceeds anyway: a parent with a `*.` alias means two Traefik routes match the new name, MongoDB has no CREATE DATABASE, and a database of that name already existing means it will be used rather than created.

args.name: string
args.options: { newBranch?: boolean, name?: string, database?: 'none' | 'create' | 'copy', instance?: string }?

worktree_create.why: N — the item nothing else in this space does. `git worktree add` gives a branch its own directory; this gives that directory its own subdomain, its own database and its own environment, so two branches of one application run side by side.
worktree_create.notes: Plans first and refuses on the plan's own reason, so the command and the preview cannot disagree. Steps in order, each rolling back the ones before it: git worktree add (streamed as scaffold:progress / scaffold:done, the same events project_clone uses), then the manifest, then the database, then the record, then the generate. NOTHING IS WRITTEN INTO THE CHECKOUT THAT GIT TRACKS — the files in a worktree are the branch's. Identity goes into stackvo.local.json, the machine-local overlay that exists to be the file that is never committed, and which is added to the repository's .git/info/exclude (git's own per-clone ignore list, never .gitignore) when git says it is not ignored yet. A branch that carries no stackvo.json gets a full one derived from the parent's instead, with the parent's aliases and LAN sharing dropped so it cannot claim the same names. The environment — database credentials, APP_URL, STACKVO_WORKTREE_BRANCH — is app-owned, outside every checkout, and reaches the container through the compose overlay site.rs already renders. The database is a database on an instance that is already running, not an instance of its own: a branch is not a different engine. Emits project:creating / project:created, because a worktree IS a project and nothing downstream knows the word. Audited as worktree_create.

args.name: string
args.options: { force?: boolean, dropDatabase?: boolean, deleteBranch?: boolean }?

worktree_remove.why: The way back. A worktree left behind is a directory that looks like a project, a branch git will not check out anywhere else, and a database nothing points at.
worktree_remove.notes: Four things can go and three of them are separate decisions the screen asks first: the checkout always, its uncommitted changes (`force`), its database (`dropDatabase`) and its branch (`deleteBranch`). Order is the reverse of creation with one exception — the containers go first, because Docker holds the tree open through its bind mount and git refuses to remove a worktree files are being written into. The database is dropped before the checkout: one that will not drop should leave the worktree there to try again from, rather than leaving a database nothing points at. `db::drop_database` refuses the instance's own database and the engines' system databases whatever the record says. Deleting the branch is best effort and never fatal — the worktree is already gone by then, and refusing to finish over an unmerged branch would leave the removal half done. project_delete reaching a worktree through the ordinary Delete button forgets the record and prunes git's registration, and deliberately leaves the branch and the database alone: `removeFiles` is that command's only licence to destroy anything. Audited as worktree_remove.

worktree_env_set.returns: { env: Record<string, string>, effective: Record<string, string> }
worktree_env_set.why: A worktree's own environment variables. site_save cannot serve this: it writes .stackvo/site.json, which is inside the checkout, and on a worktree the checkout is a branch somebody else is working on.
worktree_env_set.notes: Keys and values go through the same checks the project overlay applies (site::checked_key / checked_value) — a POSIX variable name, and a value with no line break in it, because the overlay is YAML and a newline in a scalar is a second directive somebody else wrote. `effective` is what the container will actually be given: the derived database variables and APP_URL beside the typed ones, with DB_PASSWORD masked and the same password masked inside DATABASE_URL. The credentials are never stored in the record — they are derived from the instance on every render, so a password changed in Settings reaches every worktree at the next generate instead of leaving a stale copy. A typed variable of the same name still wins, which is what makes the derived ones a default rather than a decision.

project_create.notes: Writes the manifest, runs generate, then builds. The build half is what makes it an operation rather than a mutation.

project_delete.notes: remove_files is NEW and MUST default to false. The current deleteProject() removes the project directory outright with no confirmation contract — a desktop app deleting user source code needs an explicit opt-in. The flag guards the user's CODE and nothing else: deleting a project always removes its container (web, worker sidecars, tunnel), every image tagged stackvo-<name>, generated/projects/<name>, logs/projects/<name>, its /etc/hosts line if StackVo wrote it, and its name from the certificate — all of which exist only because the project did. Docker-side cleanup is best effort and logged: a stopped engine is a fine moment to stop managing a project, and making the daemon a lock on deletion would be worse than a leftover image. Traefik needs nothing extra — project routing is compose labels, so it goes with the regenerated compose file. Named volumes likewise: a project service declares only bind mounts. Build cache is NOT touched; it is shared and global, and pruning it belongs to docker_prune.

project_dockerfile_preview.why: Runs the Rust generator port alongside the Bash one so its output can be compared before it replaces anything. `matchesBashOutput` is the differential check, live against the user's own projects rather than only against fixtures.
project_dockerfile_preview.notes: Strict mode is the behaviour change made visible: where Bash silently drops an incompatible extension, this refuses and names it. `skipped` always reports what compat mode would have dropped, so the difference is legible either way.

project_get.why: ProjectDetail.vue currently re-fetches the whole list and filters client-side.

project_local_read.why: B-2. A committed manifest is what makes a checkout reproducible and is exactly why there was nowhere to say “on this machine, PHP 8.3”. Reads the overlay beside it.

project_local_write.why: Text rather than a parsed object: this is a file somebody types, and a struct round-trip would reformat what they wrote. Empty text removes the file — “no overrides” and “an empty overrides file” are the same state and only one of them is something to wonder about in a directory listing. MUST reject `name` and `runtime`, and MUST validate the merged document rather than the fragment.

project_hooks_plan.returns: HookPlan[] — one per event, in lifecycle order
project_hooks_plan.why: B-3. A hook is a command from a repository somebody cloned, so what would run has to be readable before it does.

project_hooks_approve.why: Approves this project's HOST commands exactly as they are now. The digest is sent back rather than recomputed server-side, and that round trip is the point: it is a receipt for the list the person actually read. MUST refuse when the manifest changed between the screen being drawn and the button being pressed — that refusal is what makes this consent rather than a checkbox. Container steps are never gated: the container already runs the repository's code.

project_hooks_revoke.why: Withdraws approval. Takes no digest — you may always revoke.

project_manifest_write.why: Editing an existing project is impossible today — the UI can only create and delete. MUST honour the write rules in project.schema.json (extensions last, one runtime block).

args.service: string? (database service id; omit for dumps only)

request_timeline.why: F-2, whose note read 'dump/mail/log three separate screens, no correlation'. What the code thought it had (dd()) and what it actually asked the database for are two halves of one question, and reading them meant comparing clocks by eye across two panes.
request_timeline.notes: Dumps correlate: the bridge writes the request they happened in, so several from one page load group together and the group is named. Queries do NOT — MySQL's general log records the statement and the connection and nothing about which HTTP request caused it, and guessing from adjacency would be wrong on the first concurrent request and wrong silently. They are placed by time and left ungrouped, and the screen says which is which. Attributing a query to a request needs the application to say so, which is code inside somebody's project — the thing this feature exists to avoid needing. A database that cannot be reached yields the dumps alone rather than an error. See src-tauri/src/timeline.rs.

profiler_tree.why: F-3. `profiler_read` answers where the time went — a table of the costliest functions — and cannot answer what called that, which is the question a flame view exists for. The parser was already reading caller→callee edges to attribute inclusive cost and was discarding the caller.
profiler_tree.notes: A call TREE, not strictly a flame graph, and the difference is stated rather than glossed: a flame graph is built from sampled stacks, so a box's width is how often that exact path appeared. Cachegrind holds no stacks — it holds edges summed over every place A called B. A function called from two places is one box here with the total, two boxes there. What a branch means is 'reaching B through A cost this much in total', which is answerable and is the question people bring to a profile; 'this path was taken this often' is not, and no arrangement of the edges recovers it. Separate from profiler_read because the tree is thousands of nodes and the table is sixty rows. Recursion stops at the first repeat on the path and the frame is kept and marked. See src-tauri/src/profile.rs.

profiler_flame.why: F-3, and the reason the word flame graph can now be used. profiler_tree draws what cachegrind holds — the SUMMED cost of "A called B" over every place A called B — so a function reached from two callers is one box carrying both, and no arrangement of those edges recovers which caller was expensive. An Xdebug trace holds every entry and exit with its depth, which is a stack: folding those gives one box per distinct path, with its own measured width. MUST be a separate command from profiler_tree rather than a flag on it, because the two are different claims about the same picture and a reader cannot tell them apart by looking.

query_log.why: F-1, and §2 called it the largest product gap: three competitors sell query logging and N+1 detection, and this stack could not say what the database had been asked. The row also said it needed a collector inside the container — for MySQL and MariaDB that is wrong, and this is why.
query_log.notes: All four databases this app runs, each switched on at runtime with no agent, no rebuild and no code in the application. MySQL and MariaDB point their general log at a TABLE with two SET GLOBAL statements; Mongo profiles per database; Postgres takes three ALTER SYSTEM statements and a reload, which pin the switch, an epoch-stamped line prefix and the destination format. Reading Postgres back means asking the server where it writes — pg_current_logfile() — rather than assuming the container's stdout: every StackVo Postgres package ships logging_collector = on, which takes stderr away from the stream and puts it in a file under the data directory. Anything that is not a database answers supported:false rather than an error, because 'not this kind' must not read as 'something broke'. Verified against this workspace's live mysql:9.7, mariadb:12.3, postgres:14 and mongo:8.0 by examples/querylog_probe.rs. See src-tauri/src/querylog.rs.

query_log_record.why: The log records every statement unsampled and costs write throughput, so it is an instrument you switch on, look at, and switch off — never a default.
query_log_record.notes: One command with a boolean rather than two, because the pair is one decision and the interesting failure is leaving it on. Stopping also clears: what the log holds is statement text, and in a development database an INSERT carries the row. MySQL truncates the table and Mongo drops the collection; Postgres cannot, because the log is the server's own file, so stopping writes the same watermark query_log_clear does and nothing this app shows reaches back past it. Nothing is written to disk by the app and nothing reaches a diagnostics bundle — on Postgres the server itself keeps what it wrote, which the pane says while recording.

query_log_clear.why: Start again from here — what somebody presses before reloading the page they are investigating. Without it every read is the whole session and the one request under study is buried.
query_log_clear.notes: A deletion on three of the four: MySQL truncates mysql.general_log, Mongo drops system.profile. Postgres deletes nothing — the log belongs to the server and this app must not rewrite it — and used to answer with a no-op, which is the same reply as success and was hidden by hiding the button. It now writes a watermark statement, and the reader drops everything above it. 'Cannot delete' was never the same as 'cannot start again'.

project_lan_share.why: E-3. `shop.loc` exists in exactly one place — this machine's /etc/hosts — so opening the site on a real phone has never been possible without editing a file on that phone. This writes the intent; `lan_status` derives the name.
project_lan_share.notes: Writes `lan_share` and nothing else. The hostname is NOT stored: sslip.io resolves an address out of the name arithmetically, so the name is computed from whatever this machine's address is at the moment it is asked for — a stored one would survive a DHCP lease and point at whichever machine took it next. Regeneration is still the caller's, exactly as it is for every other manifest change; a switch that quietly rebuilt the workspace would be doing an expensive thing behind a cheap-looking control.

lan_status.why: The screen has to be able to say three different things: here is the address a phone can use, this machine has no address to offer, and the name baked into the compose file is from a network this laptop is no longer on.
lan_status.notes: `address` is null both when there is no network and when the address is public — the second is a refusal, because handing out `shop.<public-ip>.sslip.io` would publish a development site under a name anybody can resolve. `stale` reads the rendered compose file rather than recomputing: the question is whether what was written still matches what would be written. The certificate is the local CA's and the visiting device does not trust it, so its browser warns; that is a missing trust anchor on a device this app cannot reach, not a fault it can fix. See src-tauri/src/lan.rs.

oauth_callbacks.returns: { path: string, local: string | null, public: string | null, providers: Array<{ id: string, label: string, accepts: 'any' | 'publiconly', note: string }> }
oauth_callbacks.why: M-12, which sat on the list as 'an OAuth callback for .loc' and was not defined enough to build. Reading what the providers require settles it: a redirect URI is a BROWSER REDIRECT, not a fetch — the provider sends a 302 and never resolves the hostname — so https://shop.loc/auth/callback works for the flow, because the browser is on this machine, the name is in this machine's hosts file and the certificate is issued by a CA it trusts. What varies is whether the provider will accept the string at REGISTRATION time, and that is a per-provider rule that is invisible at their console.
oauth_callbacks.notes: Implements no OAuth: no client, no token exchange, and no store for a secret — the application being developed does all of that, and an app that held somebody's client secret to be helpful would be one more place for it to leak from. Returns two strings and the rule for choosing between them. The tunnel URL is read live inside the command rather than passed in, because a quick tunnel's address changes on every start and a callback registered from a stale one fails at the last step of a flow with an error naming neither side. `path` is normalised — leading slash added, duplicate slashes collapsed — and a query string or fragment is REFUSED rather than stripped: most providers compare the registered URI to the redirect exactly. See src-tauri/src/oauth.rs.

landing_status.returns: { running: boolean, container: string, url: string, rendered: string | null, projects: number, services: number }
landing_status.why: M-4. Every rival in the category ships one and it is the address people bookmark. StackVo has had the NAME for it since the beginning with nothing answering on it: core_domains already writes the bare suffix into the hosts file and certs::required_domains already issues for it, so opening https://<suffix> got Traefik's own 404 — a name the app went out of its way to make resolve, serving nothing.
landing_status.notes: `rendered` is read off the file's own timestamp rather than remembered, so an app restart, a hand-edited page and a workspace copied from another machine all stay truthful. A project with no domain is left OFF the page rather than listed as an unclickable row. A sidecar in the shape tunnel_start already established: one `docker run` on the stack network with Traefik labels, --rm so stopping is removal. The generated compose file is deliberately untouched — it is compared byte for byte against the Bash generator's output, and a service only this app knows about would break that comparison for a page. nginx:alpine rather than the alpine:3 this app already pulls, because Alpine's busybox is built WITHOUT the httpd applet (measured: `httpd: applet not found`). The page is one static file with no scripts, no fonts and no requests of its own — a landing page that needs the network to render is blank exactly when something is wrong — and every name on it is HTML-escaped, because a project is a directory and a directory can be called `R&D`. Measured end to end with examples/landing_probe.rs: the container is started against the live stack, https://stackvo.loc is requested with the system trust store and no --insecure, and the bytes that come back are compared with the bytes that were written; the container and the scratch directory are removed either way.

landing_refresh.why: The sidecar serves a FILE, so starting a project after the page was written leaves it stale with nothing having stopped. Rewriting is therefore a different action from serving, and one button doing both would restart a container to update a list.
landing_refresh.notes: Writes atomically into generated/landing/index.html and returns the fresh status. Safe to call while the container is running: nginx serves whatever is on disk at request time and the mount is read-only from its side.

landing_start.why: An operation rather than a mutation: the first start pulls nginx, which belongs in the operation console rather than behind a frozen button.
landing_start.notes: Renders the page BEFORE starting the container — nginx answers 403 for an empty directory, which reads as a broken proxy rather than as a page that has not been written yet. A sidecar in the shape tunnel_start already established: one `docker run` on the stack network with Traefik labels, --rm so stopping is removal. The generated compose file is deliberately untouched — it is compared byte for byte against the Bash generator's output, and a service only this app knows about would break that comparison for a page. nginx:alpine rather than the alpine:3 this app already pulls, because Alpine's busybox is built WITHOUT the httpd applet (measured: `httpd: applet not found`). The page is one static file with no scripts, no fonts and no requests of its own — a landing page that needs the network to render is blank exactly when something is wrong — and every name on it is HTML-escaped, because a project is a directory and a directory can be called `R&D`. Measured end to end with examples/landing_probe.rs: the container is started against the live stack, https://stackvo.loc is requested with the system trust store and no --insecure, and the bytes that come back are compared with the bytes that were written; the container and the scratch directory are removed either way.

landing_stop.why: Turning it off has to be as easy as turning it on.
landing_stop.notes: `--rm` means stopping is removal, so nothing is left answering on the name after the page is switched off.

project_register.why: project_adopt refuses a directory that already has a stackvo.json, and refuses correctly — it must not overwrite settings somebody chose. But that was only half an answer: the compose files, the hosts entry and the certificate had not happened either, and nothing else did them. The manifest watcher reports a change and regenerates nothing, on purpose.
project_register.notes: The other half. Reads and schema-checks the manifest that is already there, generates, syncs the hosts entry and the certificate, and writes nothing back — a committed manifest is the team's answer, and the Manifest tab is where it changes. Refuses when there is no stackvo.json, because that is adoption's job. Fixes the manual case too: a repository cloned into projects/ by hand with its manifest committed was skipped by project_adoptable and rejected by project_adopt, so it never came online at all.

project_requirements.returns: { declared: Array<{ id: string, known: boolean, enabled: boolean }>, suggested: Array<{ service: string, key: string }>, plan: Plan }
project_requirements.why: Competitive review B-1: herd.yml, .lerd.yaml and .ddev/config.yaml all describe the whole environment and are committed, so a teammate clones and runs one command. stackvo.json carried the project and a preset carried the stack, and the two never met. `services` in the manifest is the missing half; this reports what the repository declares, what this machine gives it, and the diff.
project_requirements.notes: Reads only. `declared` comes from the manifest — the statement a colleague agreed to — and `suggested` from the project's own .env, which is a guess and is kept separate for that reason; suggestions already declared are dropped. A suggestion carries the KEY that implied it and never the value, because that file holds credentials. `plan` is produced by the same planner preset_plan uses, so an unknown service id is rejected there by name rather than becoming a SERVICE_<JUNK>_ENABLE key. See src-tauri/src/detect.rs `services_from_env` for what counts as evidence.

project_requirements_apply.why: Turns the declaration into an enabled stack, through the plan-then-apply path a preset import already uses rather than a second one with its own rules.
project_requirements_apply.notes: Writes .env and stops, exactly as preset_apply does: the returned plan says needsRegenerate and regenerating is a visible step with its own progress. Never disables anything — a project declares what it needs, and one project not needing Redis is not a statement that another project's Redis should stop. Never writes a version: there is one SERVICE_<NAME>_VERSION per workspace, so a project pinning one would change every other project's database. Re-plans inside the call, so a .env changed between the review and the click is not overwritten with a stale diff.

project_requirements_declare.why: Writes the `services` list into stackvo.json, which is the file that gets committed — the point of the feature is that the next person to clone does not have to be told.
project_requirements_declare.notes: Reads the manifest, replaces one list and writes it back, so a field this version of the UI does not know about cannot be lost on the round trip. Ids are trimmed, lower-cased and de-duplicated the same way manifest::read normalises them. An unknown id is a WARNING and not an error: an invalid manifest is a project the app refuses to build, and a typo in an optional field must not take a project offline.

project_scaffold.why: The create half of P0-1 (detection/adoption shipped first). Runs the framework's own installer in a throwaway container — composer create-project, wp-cli, create-next-app — so nothing is installed on the host and only the bind-mounted project directory survives.
project_scaffold.notes: Ends where adoption begins: the UI follows with project_adopt, which detects runtime/server/document root from what the installer actually wrote — the same machinery as a git clone. Nine installers, every command pinned non-interactive — each flag measured against a real container rather than read off a README (nuxi needs both --template and --force; sv needs --no-add-ons; astro needs --yes). The JavaScript ones pass --no-install: the node Dockerfile installs for the container's platform, and a host node_modules in the image is the arm64-in-amd64 mistake NODE_DOCKERIGNORE exists to prevent (a prompt inside an operation console is a hang, not a question). On unix runs --user uid:gid so files land owned by the user, not root. Refuses a non-empty directory; a failed install that wrote nothing removes the husk so the retry is not blocked. Seventeen installers now, across PHP, JavaScript, Python and Ruby. Composer projects carry --ignore-platform-reqs because the installer container is not the machine the code runs on (CakePHP wants ext-intl, the composer image has none, and StackVo's PHP image does); Rails needs the full ruby image rather than slim, which cannot compile websocket-driver. Twenty-eight templates in two kinds: an installer container where the ecosystem has a scaffolder, and **written files** where it does not — Gin, Echo, Flask, FastAPI, Sinatra and Rocket are each 'write two files and let the language build them', so pulling an image to write thirty lines would be a download for nothing. Their dependencies are not skipped, they move: the project's own Dockerfile already runs pip/go build/bundle/cargo for the container's platform. Every written template binds 0.0.0.0 on the port lang_defaults gives its runtime — a test asserts it over code lines only, because the comments explaining the loopback trap were tripping the check.

project_validate.why: Pre-flight the new-project form against project.schema.json + php-extensions.json before anything touches disk. Today a bad extension name is only discovered when the Docker build fails minutes later.

pty_open.v1Change: PtyTarget is NEW: { kind: 'container', name } or { kind: 'host', cwd }. node-pty could only reach containers because it ran inside one; portable-pty on the host can open a real host shell in the project directory.

quick_command_run.notes: **The fixed catalog is the security model.** The frontend sends an ID, never a command; the argv is built on the Rust side from compiled-in words, so there is no code path by which the webview can name a program to execute — the same handle-not-a-path rule app_log_open uses, for the same reason: a project pane that accepted an arbitrary command string from its own frontend is a remote shell with extra steps. Every command is spawned as an argv ARRAY, never through a shell, so a project called `a; rm -rf ~` is a container name that does not exist rather than a second command. Two kinds, because they behave differently: interactive commands (tinker, wp shell) need a TTY and a human, so they open the user's own terminal and return null — an in-app REPL would be a second, worse one next to the one they have configured; one-shot commands stream through the operation console. `-it` is added only for the interactive ones, because Docker refuses `-t` when stdin is not a TTY. Refuses when the container is not running, so the failure is "the project is not running" rather than Docker's "No such container". B-4: the id may now name a command the project declared in its own stackvo.json as well as one compiled in. The webview still never names a program — `quickcmd::resolve` is the only place either becomes an argv, and a declared command reaches `docker exec` through the same function a built-in does.

quick_commands.why: P3-19 was "a tinker quick action — the PTY exists, so it is nearly free". It is, and on its own it is also one button. What is worth building is the set it belongs to: artisan tinker, artisan migrate, composer install, npm install, wp shell. Each of those today means opening a terminal, remembering the container name and typing `docker exec -it stackvo-<project> …`.
quick_commands.notes: Offered only when the marker file exists — driven off the same Fingerprint adoption uses, so "does this project have artisan" is answered in one place. Offering a command the project cannot run is worse than omitting it: the failure arrives as `artisan: not found` in an operation console, which reads as a broken app rather than as a button that never applied. `because` names the file the offer is based on. Deliberately ABSENT: migrate:fresh, migrate:reset, db:wipe and composer update — the first three drop the user's data behind a button four characters from the safe one, and the last rewrites a lock file. Those are things to type deliberately in the terminal that is one click away. M-9 adds the four frameworks this app scaffolds and did not offer a row for: Symfony (bin/console), Django (manage.py), Rails and plain Ruby. Each is the same shape — a fixed id, an argv and a marker file only that framework writes. Rails is detected on `bin/rails` rather than on a Gemfile, which is Sinatra and Jekyll as often as it is Rails, and it runs through `bundle exec` rather than the binstub: a binstub is only executable if its permission bit survived the checkout, and `bundle exec` needs the gem rather than the bit. Doctrine's migrate carries --allow-no-migration because it exits non-zero with nothing to run, which the console would draw as a failed operation. This is NOT the B-4 unlock: B-4 is a command the WORKSPACE declares, and every row here is still compiled in. B-4: the list is the built-in catalogue filtered by the project's marker files, then whatever the project's own stackvo.json declares under `commands`, marked with `declared` so a caller can say which is which. Declared entries are container commands only — there is no `host` form, which is why this needed no approval flow; see src-tauri/src/quickcmd.rs.

repl_runners.why: F-5, and §5.5 held it as a decision rather than a task: quickcmd refused an in-app REPL in writing — "a second, worse REPL next to the one they already have configured" — and reversing a refusal is not something a commit does quietly. The refusal stands for a LINE repl and this is not one. A snippet is twenty lines you edit: write a query, run it, change line three, run it again. In tinker that is retyping. `tinker` still opens the user's own terminal, and the two are split by what the person is doing rather than ranked.
repl_runners.notes: Offered from the same Fingerprint the quick commands use. Two tiers, and each row says which it is: `booted` means the application is loaded (artisan tinker, wp eval, manage.py shell, bin/rails runner), and false means the language on its own (php -r, node -e) — a pane that showed them alike would let somebody debug for ten minutes before finding out their models were never loaded. Laravel is offered only where composer.json also declares laravel/tinker, because --execute is Tinker's flag and a --no-dev install does not have it. See src-tauri/src/repl.rs.

repl_run.why: Run the snippet against the booted application and hand back everything about the run — both streams, the exit code, the duration.
repl_run.notes: **The webview picks a runner, it never names a program.** `laravel` means `php artisan tinker --execute` and nothing else; an id outside the table is refused before anything is spawned, and so is one the project has no files for. The snippet is ONE argv element and always the LAST, so a snippet containing `; rm -rf ~` is a string rather than a second command — the rule hooks and quickcmd state as their security model. It runs in the project's own container, which already runs that repository's code, and there is no host runner: a snippet that has to run on this machine is a hook, approved against a digest first. Two limits, guarding different failures: `timeout` INSIDE the container stops the snippet (killing a docker exec client does not stop what it started), and this process's own clock stops the wait. `limited` records which — measured present in php, node, python, ruby and wordpress-cli images, but "every image I checked" is not "every image". Success is read from the exit code and never from "stderr was empty": a PHP fatal is written to stdout, measured. Laravel's --execute does not echo the last expression the way the interactive REPL does, so the pane says to dump().

repl_history.why: The snippet you ran ten minutes ago, back in the editor. Without it the workbench is a text box that forgets, which is the terminal REPL's weakness rather than an improvement on it.
repl_history.notes: The code, never the output. A snippet is what the person wrote and is the thing they want back; the output is the application's DATA — a row, a customer, a token — and querylog states the rule this follows: what came out of somebody's database is not written to disk by this app. Kept in the app's own config directory beside hook-consent.json, never in the project, because a file written into a checkout turns up in somebody's git status. A re-run moves a snippet back to the top rather than adding a copy.

repl_history_clear.why: Forget them. A snippet can hold a customer's id or a token somebody pasted in, and a history with no way to clear it is one people learn not to use.

release_build.notes: **Verification is not optional and not a separate button.** The safety property here — no .env in the image, no active debugger — is exactly the kind that is easy to state in a Dockerfile and quietly wrong in the result, so the built image is RUN and asked. Proven both ways on a real project: with the ignore file, zero env files; without it, all five of that project's .env.* land in a layer and the check names every one. `hasApp` catches the other silent failure — a build whose context was empty produces an image that starts and serves nothing, which otherwise looks like a success. The ignore file is written BESIDE the generated Dockerfile as `Dockerfile.dockerignore`, which BuildKit reads in preference to the context's — confirmed to work before anything depended on it — so building somebody's image writes nothing into their repository. The tag is validated before it reaches a command line: lowercase only, because Docker rejects an uppercase repository with an error that does not say so.

release_load.returns: string[] (the image names the daemon adopted)
release_load.notes: `docker load` — the return trip `release_save` never had, and the half of an air-gapped install that was missing. Takes no project name and needs no workspace: a bundle is loaded on the machine that received it, which is exactly the machine that may have neither. A missing file is answered NOT_FOUND here rather than being handed to Docker, which calls it an invalid archive and sends the user looking for a corrupt bundle instead of a wrong path. The names come from `docker load`'s own stdout because nothing else knows them — the file name is whatever somebody called it, and one stream can carry several images. An image with no tag is reported by id rather than dropped: it did load, and an empty answer reads as an empty bundle.

release_plan.why: P3-20 — what `laradock ship` does. The analysis calls it the long-horizon differentiator because the container lineage makes it possible and no native-binary competitor can follow. It is also the item with a real question inside it, answered by looking at what the images actually contain rather than by assuming.
release_plan.notes: **The dev image is not a production image**, measured on this checkout: a PHP project's image holds NO application code — /var/www/html contains one file, index.nginx-debian.html, because the source arrives through a bind mount — and it has Xdebug loaded. Exporting it ships a web server with nothing to serve and a step debugger that dials out on every request. A NODE image is the opposite: its Dockerfile does COPY . . and npm install, so it already holds the code and the build. Hence two strategies: `layer` (build FROM the dev image, add the source, remove the debugger inis) and `retag` (nothing to add; rebuilding would replace a Linux node_modules with whatever the host has). `excluded` carries every ignore pattern WITH ITS REASON, because an exclusion the user cannot explain is one they work around. `warnings` names what the result will be true of — no .env, vendor as it is on disk, Xdebug's binary still present though inactive — before the build rather than after.

release_push_plan.why: H-1. MUST re-run the verification rather than remember it from the build: the interval between building and pushing is exactly where somebody could retag something else onto the name.

release_push.why: MUST re-check on the way out — the plan the caller was shown crossed the IPC boundary and came back, and a check that only runs on the way out is not a check.

release_recipe.why: A deployment recipe for the built image. Returned as TEXT, not written: where it belongs is the user's decision. MUST carry no source mount, no debugger, no database container, and variable NAMES with empty values — a recipe with credentials in it is a .env wearing a different extension, and this file is meant to be committed.

release_save.notes: `docker save` to a tarball — the artefact you hand to something that is not this machine.

secret_move.why: On a company machine ~/.stackvo/.env is backed up, synced and DLP-scanned, and it holds database passwords in plain text (readiness review §5.2). This moves one into Keychain / Credential Manager / Secret Service and leaves `keychain:<entry>` in its place.
secret_move.notes: One key at a time and never automatic, because it has a consequence: the Bash CLI reads .env directly and would use the string `keychain:…` as the password. Writes the keystore first and the .env line second, and removes the entry again if the file write fails — the other order loses the password. Moving an already-moved key succeeds silently rather than failing, so a double click is not an error. Errors: INVALID_INPUT for a key that is not a credential, NOT_FOUND when there is no value to move, PERMISSION_DENIED when the keystore will not open. Audited as `secret_move`. This does NOT remove the value from generated/docker-compose.dynamic.yml, which is rendered with the real password — see docs/durum.md §6, decision 0010.

secret_restore.why: The way back. A user may only discover the CLI incompatibility after moving a key, and without this the only way out is hand-editing .env with a value the app will not show them.
secret_restore.notes: Writes the .env line first and deletes the keystore entry second — deleting first and failing to write would destroy the password. The only caller of env_writer::apply_verbatim, which is what stops the ordinary write path from undoing a move nobody asked to undo. Audited as `secret_restore`.

secrets_status.returns: { available: boolean, keys: Array<{ key: string, moved: boolean, resolvable: boolean, set: boolean }> }
secrets_status.why: The Settings pane has to draw a row per credential saying where it lives, and it has to know before it offers a Move button whether this machine has a keystore at all — a headless Linux box with no Secret Service is a real machine somebody runs this on.
secrets_status.notes: Reads the .env text, NOT a loaded Env: loading replaces a keychain: reference with the value it points at, which is exactly the fact this reports. `available` is probed by reading an entry nothing ever writes, so asking leaves nothing behind. No value ever appears in the response — `env_reveal` remains the one deliberate way a password crosses the boundary. See src-tauri/src/secrets.rs.

server_config_get.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
server_config_get.notes: The raw file including its comments. Only nginx and caddy are accepted; the other servers have no generated config file for a snippet to be added to.

server_config_set.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
server_config_set.notes: Written atomically. Takes effect on the next generate: the directives are rendered into each project's server config, not into a file the server reads directly.

service_connection.why: The services sheet showed a container name, a port table and a credentials block, and left the reader to assemble a URI. The obvious assembly — `mongodb://stackvo-mongo:27017/` — cannot work from the host, because that name only resolves on the Docker network. Null for a service nobody connects to with a string.
service_connection.notes: Two addresses come back, not one: `fromHost` is 127.0.0.1 and the published port, `fromContainer` is the container name and the port inside it. `fromHost` is null when a running container publishes nothing, rather than an address that would fail. The password is bullets unless `reveal` — the same act `env_reveal` is, and percent-encoded on the Rust side so a password containing `@` cannot rename the host. See src-tauri/src/connect.rs.

service_db_clients.why: The picker beside `service_open_in_client` has to be built from what is on this machine, not from a list of clients somebody might have. Empty for most services, which is the answer rather than a failure: a service with no connection string has nothing to open, and an AMQP or SMTP address is not one a desktop database client takes.
service_db_clients.notes: Which protocols a client opens is read from the application rather than declared here — on macOS from the bundle's own CFBundleURLTypes. That is not a detail: Redis Insight declares only `redisinsight`, so a table written from the name would have offered it for `redis://` and produced a button that launches an app which ignores the address. An installed client that does not declare the scheme is omitted rather than greyed out — it is not missing, it is not applicable. The first entry is always the system handler, with the empty id. See src-tauri/src/apps.rs.

args.client: string (id from service_db_clients; empty = the system handler)

service_open_in_client.why: G-3. The correct connection string has existed since connect.rs was written and the sheet has offered to copy it since; what was missing was the step that pastes it, which everybody was doing by hand.
service_open_in_client.notes: Always the host address — the container one is a name on a Docker network that no client on this desktop can resolve, which is the confusion connect.rs exists to remove. Refuses when the container publishes nothing rather than inventing 127.0.0.1. The URI carries the real password, because a URI with bullets in it is one that fails to connect, so this is `reveal` in the sense of env_reveal and is recorded in the audit trail as one — the service and the client, never the URI. The cost is that the secret is an argument to `open` and so visible in `ps` while that process lives; the alternative is a temporary file with the same reachability and a lifetime nobody controls. Copying the string is still there for a shared machine.

service_dependencies.notes: Kept for completeness; services_list already returns required/optional/unmetDependencies per service, so the front end has no reason to call this separately.

service_reveal.why: The value behind one masked credential on the services list, whichever place this workspace keeps it.
service_reveal.notes: Dispatches the way every other reader of service state does — the instance table when there is one, `.env` when there is not. `key` is the manifest setting key for an instance (`ROOT_PASSWORD`) and the `.env` key for the legacy path (`SERVICE_MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`), which is what the row carries in each case. The detail sheet called `env_reveal` directly before this existed, and after a handover that reported "not set in .env" over a password that does exist.

system_accent.returns: { available: boolean, name: string|null, hex: string|null }
system_accent.why: The desktop's own accent colour, so the app can match it instead of shipping a brand colour that clashes with everyone's system theme.
system_accent.notes: macOS reads AppleHighlightColor via `defaults` and maps it to the eight colours the OS itself draws with. Elsewhere `available` is false and both fields are null — Windows keeps its accent in the registry, and saying "unknown" beats returning a wrong blue. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

template_override.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
template_override.notes: Copies the shipped file into the workspace so it can be edited, and returns its absolute path. Refuses when a copy is already there — that file is the user's edit. Only paths in templates_list are accepted.

template_revert.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
template_revert.notes: Deletes the workspace's copy; the version in the binary takes over on the next render. Destructive and not undoable — the front end confirms first.

templates_list.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
templates_list.notes: Every template compiled into the binary, with whether this workspace has a copy on disk. Installing writes none, so a copy means somebody chose to override it.

terminal_open_external.v1Change: Always works. The HTTP version returned HTTP 400 with 'Terminal cannot be opened from containerized environment' — it could never succeed in the shipped configuration.

args.labels: Record<string,string>? (keeps the current catalog when omitted)

tray_relabel.notes: Re-label the tray and the native menu bar, and adopt the catalog they are drawn from. The tray is created during setup(), before the webview exists, so Rust carries a fallback table for the two languages this build was born with — but that table is a bootstrap detail, not the app's translation of its own tray. The front end sends the real strings on boot and on every language change, which is what stops a third language from being a change to tray.rs. A map rather than a named type on purpose: a struct would make every new menu entry a contract change on top of a code change. The keys are checked instead — a catalog missing any of them is refused with INVALID_INPUT naming the gaps, because a menu half in one language reads as broken rather than untranslated. The three counted labels (containers, more, runningSummary) arrive as templates carrying {count} / {running} / {total}: Rust knows the numbers, the language file decides where they go.

tunnel_start.why: Starts a cloudflared quick-tunnel sidecar on the stack's network, forwarding a random trycloudflare.com URL to the project's container. No account, no token — and no host-binary competitor can attach to the container network at all.
tunnel_start.notes: An operation because the first start pulls the cloudflared image, which can take minutes. Targets the project container directly (with the local domain as Host header): with SSL on, every Traefik project router is websecure-only, which a public visitor cannot handshake against. Refuses when the project container is not running — a tunnel serving 502s looks like it worked. The URL that results is public and unauthenticated while the tunnel runs; the UI says so.

tunnel_status.why: Webhook testing (Stripe, GitHub) had no answer: myapp.loc does not exist on the internet. This reports every running tunnel sidecar and its assigned public URL.
tunnel_status.notes: The URL is read from the sidecar's own log on every call rather than cached — what the log says is what is actually live, across app restarts and container crashes alike. `url` is null while cloudflared is still connecting; the UI polls until it appears.

tunnel_stop.notes: The sidecar runs with --rm, so stop is also removal — nothing is left behind to leak the old URL.

updater_status.returns: { configured: boolean, hasPublicKey: boolean, endpoints: number }
updater_status.notes: Whether this build can verify an update. Tauri checks a bundle's signature against the public key compiled into the app; with an empty `pubkey` every check fails inside the plugin with a message about signatures, which reads like a server fault and is a build fault. Read from tauri.conf.json via include_str! so the answer describes the binary, not the working tree.

updates_check.notes: Needs tauri-plugin-updater plus a signing key and a release endpoint — i.e. a release pipeline, not just code. Deferred to Phase 4 alongside signed builds. Declared here so the surface is complete and the gap is visible.

window_close_action.notes: Carries out the choice the close dialog collected, optionally storing it as closeBehaviour. Four behaviours exist including "ask"; the extra "quit" (close, leave the stack running) is meaningful here because the containers are Docker's and outlive the app.

worker_options.why: Which workers this project can offer, from its files alone: artisan offers 'queue' and 'scheduler', laravel/horizon in composer.json adds 'horizon'. A Node project gets an empty list, not an error.

worker_start.notes: The sidecar runs the project's own image (same PHP, extensions, bind mount and network, so .env and the database resolve as the web container sees them) with --restart unless-stopped — self-healing is Docker's own supervisor, not reimplemented. queue:work carries --max-time=3600 on purpose: a worker holds the code it booted with, and an hour caps how long it serves yesterday's code. Refuses when the project has no built container.

worker_status.why: A Laravel app runs queue:work, the scheduler and Horizon beside the web server; locally they live in a forgotten terminal tab, which is why "my job never ran" is a support staple. This reports every worker sidecar with its restart count — the self-heal made visible; a large number is a crash loop, not a success story.

worker_stop.notes: Removal, not just stop: with unless-stopped, a merely-stopped container is one engine restart away from coming back.

workspace_get.why: The web UI never needed this — it ran inside the StackVo repo, so its root was `/app` by mount. A desktop app has to be told, or work it out. Returns the resolved root plus how it was resolved, so the UI can show the user which checkout it is driving.

workspace_pick.notes: Opens the native directory picker, then applies workspace_set. Returns null if the user cancels.

workspace_set.notes: Validates that the path contains core/cli/stackvo.sh and projects/ before accepting it, then persists it. Rejects with NO_WORKSPACE and an explanation rather than silently accepting a wrong folder.

xdebug_set.why: One switch instead of three manual steps: adding the extension to the manifest, configuring the client host and port, and telling the IDE where the code is mounted.
xdebug_set.notes: Writes `php.extensions` in the manifest and re-renders `generated/docker-compose.xdebug.yml`. The extension is COMPILED IN, so enabling it needs a rebuild before it takes effect — `needsRebuild` says so rather than letting the toggle look finished. Writing the manifest canonicalises it the same way project_manifest_write does (`webserver` becomes `server`); that is the contract's rule for writers, not a side effect of this command.

xdebug_status.why: Step debugging is the thing Docker makes hardest and the thing a PHP developer needs most. `xdebug` was already in the extension catalog with per-version pecl pins, so it could be compiled in by hand-editing stackvo.json — and then it still would not connect, because nothing set xdebug.mode or told it which host the IDE is on. This reports all three layers separately: listed in the manifest, present in the built image, and live in the running container.
xdebug_status.notes: `active` is read from the running container's environment rather than assumed from the manifest. The two disagree in a case users hit: `stackvo up` from the CLI does not layer the overlay this app writes, so it recreates the container without the Xdebug environment and debugging stops working with nothing on screen to explain it.

perf_export.why: The price of the feature, paid explicitly: the container reads its dependencies from a volume an editor cannot see, so autocomplete needs a copy on the host. It is a SNAPSHOT and the screen says so — the container keeps writing to the volume and this copy does not follow. Replaces the host directory rather than merging into it: a half-updated vendor/ is worse for an index than an old one, because nothing about it says which half is which.

perf_forget.why: Deletes the volume. Its own act and never part of turning the layer off — a checkbox that throws away thirty thousand files as a side effect is one nobody should trust.

perf_set.why: MUST seed the volume from the host copy BEFORE writing the setting, and MUST fail without writing it if that copy fails. A fresh named volume is empty — Docker seeds one from the image only where the image has content there, and no PHP image ships a vendor/ — so a setting saved first and a copy that failed afterwards is a site that 500s on the next request from a switch that reported success. Turning it OFF copies nothing and deletes nothing: the volume may hold the only copy of a vendor/ that took ten minutes to build. MUST refuse a path that is not relative to the project — the value becomes a container path AND part of a volume name, and it arrives from a JSON file that may have come with a git clone.

perf_status.why: I-1. A bind mount costs 2-3x a named volume on metadata and writes, which is the measured reason a Docker workflow feels slow on macOS and Windows. This lists the directories worth moving off the host filesystem for one project, whether each is currently in a volume, how big that volume is, and whether the host still has a copy for an editor to index. Suggestions describe the project in front of them — vendor for PHP, storage/framework and bootstrap/cache when it is a Laravel, node_modules when there is a package.json — and are never applied on their own.

qr_encode.returns: { version: number, size: number, rows: string[], text: string }
qr_encode.why: M-3. Two features hand out an address whose whole point is that it is opened on ANOTHER device — the LAN name from lan_status and the public URL from tunnel_status — and both are long, both contain either a dashed IP address or four random Cloudflare words, and the only way to get one onto a phone was to type it. That is the moment somebody gives up and uses the desktop browser's device emulation instead, which is not the same thing and is exactly the class of bug it fails to show.
qr_encode.notes: Byte mode, error-correction level M, versions 1-10 — 213 bytes, against a tunnel URL of about sixty. Written here rather than taken as a dependency because a QR code is a closed specification with published vectors: it cannot acquire new cases later, so the usual argument for a maintained dependency does not apply. It is NOT verified by its author's own expectations: examples/qr_probe.rs hands each symbol to macOS's own CIDetector — the decoder behind the camera — and passes a row only when the text read back is byte-identical. That measurement found the one real bug: the first format-information copy was written along row 8 instead of down column 8, and every other check passed while no decoder on earth would read the result. Returns the module matrix as one string per row rather than a picture, so the caller draws it; the front end renders an SVG with a four-module quiet zone, black on white whatever the theme is, because scanners expect dark modules on a light ground and the failure mode of an inverted code is a phone that simply sits there. INVALID_INPUT for empty text or more than a version 10 symbol holds — never a truncated symbol, which is indistinguishable from a complete one until somebody scans it. See src-tauri/src/qr.rs.

site_save.why: Whole document rather than per key: three settings in one small file, and three commands over one document is three chances for it and the screen to disagree - the same reasoning routes_save gives. MUST refuse a key that is not a POSIX variable name and a value carrying a line break: the overlay is YAML, where a newline in a scalar ends it and everything after is read as configuration somebody else wrote. Regenerates, because the directory listing lands in a GENERATED server config while the variables and the agent land in a compose overlay - two different paths for one save.

stripe_status.returns: Array<{ project: string, running: boolean, container: string, signingSecret: string | null, hasKey: boolean, failure: string | null }>
stripe_status.why: M-11. Testing a payment flow means Stripe reaching the application, and shop.loc does not exist on the internet.
stripe_status.notes: `signingSecret` and `failure` are read from the container's log on every call rather than cached, so an app restart or a crashed listener stays truthful. `hasKey` is a boolean and there is no command that reads a key back — the pane can replace it or clear it and never display it. MEASURED with examples/stripe_probe.rs against the real image and a deliberately invalid key: the image runs, the arguments are accepted, and the CLI's 401 comes back through the log reader. NOT measured, and stated rather than implied: that a real event reaches the application, which needs an account. `stripe listen` opens an OUTBOUND connection, so nothing has to be reachable from the internet — which is why this is not the tunnel with a different label: a quick tunnel's URL changes on every start, so the endpoint has to be re-registered in the dashboard each time and the signing secret changes with it. The API key is kept in the OS keystore by secrets.rs, one entry per project (two accounts must not share one, or one account's events are forwarded into the other's application, which looks like it is working). It reaches the container through `-e STRIPE_API_KEY` and never as an argument: argv is visible in `docker inspect`, in the host process list and in this app's own operation console, which streams the command it ran. The sidecar deliberately does NOT use `--rm`, unlike the tunnel's: an invalid key makes the CLI print its complaint and exit, and a removed container takes the log with it — so the pane showed no listener, no error and no reason for the single most likely failure this feature has. Found by examples/stripe_probe.rs, which also caught itself reporting success on Docker's own "No such container" message.

stripe_key_set.returns: boolean (whether a key is now stored)
stripe_key_set.why: A credential needs somewhere to go that is not a file in the workspace, and this app already decided where that is.
stripe_key_set.notes: One command for both directions: `null` clears it, because a screen that could only ADD a credential is one people are right not to give one to. A key beginning `pk_` is refused here rather than by the CLI three seconds later inside a container — a publishable key is the one somebody has open in a browser tab, and it fails with an authentication error that says nothing about which key was pasted.

stripe_start.why: An operation because the first start pulls the Stripe image.
stripe_start.notes: Refuses when the project container is not running: the CLI would otherwise accept the events, fail to deliver each one and report the failures back to Stripe, filling the dashboard with delivery errors for a project that was simply not started. Removes any previous listener before starting — the container is not `--rm`, so a crashed one still holds the name. An empty `events` list means every event, which is the CLI's own default and the right one for "does anything arrive at all". `path` is a path inside the application and a URL is refused. `stripe listen` opens an OUTBOUND connection, so nothing has to be reachable from the internet — which is why this is not the tunnel with a different label: a quick tunnel's URL changes on every start, so the endpoint has to be re-registered in the dashboard each time and the signing secret changes with it. The API key is kept in the OS keystore by secrets.rs, one entry per project (two accounts must not share one, or one account's events are forwarded into the other's application, which looks like it is working). It reaches the container through `-e STRIPE_API_KEY` and never as an argument: argv is visible in `docker inspect`, in the host process list and in this app's own operation console, which streams the command it ran. The sidecar deliberately does NOT use `--rm`, unlike the tunnel's: an invalid key makes the CLI print its complaint and exit, and a removed container takes the log with it — so the pane showed no listener, no error and no reason for the single most likely failure this feature has. Found by examples/stripe_probe.rs, which also caught itself reporting success on Docker's own "No such container" message.

stripe_stop.why: Turning it off has to be as easy as turning it on.
stripe_stop.notes: Removes rather than stops: the signing secret is in that container's log and it is dead the moment the listener is, so leaving it behind would leave a stale secret on screen for the next person to paste.

site_settings.returns: { env: Record<string,string>, directoryListing: bool, sshAgent: bool, listingSupported: bool, agentAvailable: bool, server: string }
site_settings.why: M-5, M-6 and M-10 in one document, because they are one kind of thing: a per-project setting the generator cannot read from the manifest (project.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and frozen), kept in .stackvo/site.json so it travels with the project. listingSupported and agentAvailable are answered by the machine rather than assumed by the screen: Apache and Swoole have no configuration file for a directory index, and an agent cannot be forwarded when none is running - a control drawn for either would do nothing.
