Adoptable.name: string
Adoptable.note: `has_files` ignores dotfiles: a directory holding nothing but a `.DS_Store` is empty for this purpose, and offering it for adoption as if it had code in it is how a real checkout looked before this was handled. `compose_file` is reported but NOT resolved — resolving costs a `docker compose config` per project, which is not something to spend on a list that loads on every visit; migrate_scan does that for the one the user picks.

CertPlan.note: `domains` is the exact SAN list mkcert will be invoked with, so what the user approves is what lands — the same relationship `preview` has to the hosts file. `remove` names domains the certificate still covers that no project asks for any more; they disappear on the next reissue and are listed so that is not a surprise. `rejected` names domains dropped as invalid rather than silently omitting them.
CertPlan.reloadedNote: Writing the certificate is not enough to change what a browser gets. Traefik's file provider watches generated/traefik/dynamic, and the certificates are not in it — routes.yml only points at them, and a certFile is read while the dynamic configuration is parsed. So cert_apply rewrites the watched files with their own bytes to force a reparse. Observed on a real checkout: Traefik up two days, serving a certificate a day older than the one on disk. False after an apply means the new certificate is on disk but not yet served.

CertStatus.note: `covered` is read from the certificate's subjectAltName, not from the project list. `missing` is wildcard-aware: `*.stackvo.loc` covers `api.stackvo.loc` but not `shop.loc` and not `a.b.stackvo.loc`, because a wildcard matches exactly one label. `ca_trusted` is null when the platform gives no cheap way to ask, which is not the same as false. `stale` is true when anything is missing or the certificate has expired — it is what the UI badges.

CompanionRow.name: string — the manifest's handle, and the suffix of the container name
CompanionRow.containerName: string — stackvo-<instance>-<name>, derived exactly as render::context derives it
CompanionRow.image: string — the reference actually pulled, digest-pinned when the manifest pins one

Connection.note: `masked` is false both when `reveal` was asked for and when the service has no password at all, so the UI only offers the eye where there is something behind it. `passwordKey` names the .env key rather than carrying a value — it is the same key the credentials list reveals, and the two must agree about which secret is in play.

DbTarget.note: `extension` is the suggested file extension, and it differs by engine rather than being cosmetic: mysql and postgres dump to plain SQL a person can read and edit, while mongodump produces a gzipped BSON archive that only mongorestore can read. `database` is null for mongo, where the dump covers the whole server.

DeclaredPort.name: string — the manifest's handle: main, console, smtp
DeclaredPort.host: u16? — what the container publishes when there is one, the recorded allocation when there is not

DependencyRow.capability: string — what the manifest asks for, so MariaDB can answer 'sql'
DependencyRow.service: string? — the one service that will do, when only one will
DependencyRow.provider: string? — the installed instance answering it, null when none does
DependencyRow.running: bool — false whenever there is no provider; the two are told apart by `provider`

Detected.note: `evidence` names the files the answer was read from, and `confidence` says how much to trust it. `guess` means nothing recognisable was there and the fields are defaults the user is expected to correct — presenting that as an answer is the failure this distinction exists to avoid.

DevServerStatus.note: `tool` is read from package.json with the FRAMEWORK checked before its bundler — Nuxt and Next both pull one in as a dependency, and the wrong order tells a Nuxt project to edit a vite.config.js it does not have. `command` prefers the `dev` script over `start`, because `start` in a Next project serves a production build, which is the mode this feature exists to get out of. `mounted` is read from the RUNNING container, never inferred; `stackvo up` from the Bash CLI layers three compose files, not six, and will recreate the container in production mode. `host_allowed` is null when there is no config file to look in, which is NOT the same as false — it is checked as text, because parsing JavaScript to decide whether a key is present is a much larger promise than "does the file mention it", and the answer is only ever used to decide whether to show the snippet.

DockerfilePreview.skipped: [{extension, reason}] — what the Bash generator drops without telling anyone

Flame.frames: Frame[] — folded stacks; a function under two callers is two frames
Flame.total: number — microseconds accounted for, which is the width of the root row
Flame.records: number — entry and exit records read
Flame.stacks: number — distinct stacks the file held
Flame.truncated: bool — the file was longer than the reader's ceiling; this is the start of the request
Flame.pruned: number — paths too thin to draw, dropped and counted rather than silently missing
Flame.depthCapped: bool — the stack went deeper than 64 frames
Flame.note: F-3. Microseconds always, computed by this app from the trace's own timestamps — unlike a cachegrind report, whose unit is whatever the file declares and MUST be read from it. A trace costs far more than a profile to record (two lines per function call, hundreds of megabytes for one request), which is why the mode is trigger-started like profiling and why the tree is pruned before it crosses this boundary.

Doctor.dns: { suffix: string, port: number }? — null in every ordinary state, INCLUDING the feature being off. Set only when the machine's resolver points at a local responder that is not answering: the one DNS failure nothing else on screen reports, where the app, the containers and the proxy all look healthy and every project domain fails to resolve.
Doctor.extensionsNote: **Added after reading `tools/validate-contracts.mjs`'s output instead of its summary line.** Three of that tool's four errors on this checkout are C-06 — all one root cause, `imap` removed in PHP 8.2, sitting in two project manifests AND in the stack's default extension set — and every one is local and fixable. The desktop app reported none of them, because the doctor knew about ports, disk and hosts and nothing about extensions. It matters more than a lint: the Bash generator SKIPS A BAD EXTENSION SILENTLY, so nothing fails and nothing is logged, and the symptom is a fatal `Call to undefined function imap_open()` at runtime with nothing connecting it to a build that reported success. `isDefaultSet` entries come first because they are the worse case — a project created right now, with nothing customised, cannot build. The default PHP version is itself contested (DEFAULT_PHP_VERSION vs SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES_PHP_DEFAULT, CONFLICTS.md C-12), so BOTH are checked rather than one being picked: an extension failing on either is a problem whichever key wins. Project rows reuse manifest::normalize's own C-06/C-07 findings rather than restating the rule.
Doctor.note: ports.requiredBy is the compose service that publishes the port, read from the generated files — which is the enabled set, because the generator only writes enabled services. ports.state: ok = free or held by the stack itself; warn = a docker backend holds it but the engine could not say whose container; fail = a named conflict. generated.state: warn = an input (.env or a manifest) is newer than the oldest generated compose file, detail names it; fail = never generated.

DumpsStatus.note: **There is no on/off switch, and that is deliberate.** The overlay sets VAR_DUMPER_FORMAT and VAR_DUMPER_SERVER for every eligible project and leaves them set, because with the variables set and nothing listening `dump()` renders into the response exactly as it does today — ServerDumper falls back, verified in a running container. A state file for a setting with no observable off-state would be ceremony. Two things had to hold for this to reach a WEB request rather than only the CLI, and both were checked in the container: the official PHP image's docker.conf sets `clear_env = no`, so the container environment reaches FPM workers, and `variables_order` is EGPCS — the E is what puts it in $_SERVER, which is where VarDumper looks.

Endpoint.note: `host` is 127.0.0.1 for the host address and the container name for the internal one. Both are in the URI already; they are carried separately so a client that takes a host and a port in two fields can be filled in without parsing the string back apart.

FanoutStream.note: `followed` < `total` means the 60-file cap bit and the oldest-modified files are not being watched. Reported rather than trimmed silently: a view that caps its own coverage and says nothing reads as "nothing else is happening".

FinishedEvent.subject: string
FinishedEvent.note: On failure `error` carries the last few output lines rather than a generic exit-code message — that tail is almost always the real cause.

GeneratorReport.warnings: string[] — configuration problems the port can see and StackVo does not report, e.g. C-20

HandoverNote.kind: string (resolvedMovingTag | portMoved | adoptedVolume | settingHasNoHome | unknownService | versionNotInstalled | nothingToInstall | noFreePort). `versionNotInstalled` is NOT 'unpublished': the catalogue handover reads is the local package tree, so the honest sentence is 'not installed here', and the two ask for different things — one is a click in the Market, the other is a version that was never in the index.
HandoverNote.subject: string

HandoverPreview.missing: MissingPackage[] — packages the handover needs and this machine does not have

HostsPlan.note: `preview` is the exact text that will be written — the same value the diff is rendered from, so what the user approves is what lands.

HtmlCheck.note: Percentages are of the client/feature combinations Mailpit tests (186 on the version measured against).

InstancePlan.id: string — the id this would take
InstancePlan.refused: string? — why a second instance is not allowed, or null
InstancePlan.settings: InstanceSetting[] — the manifest's, with defaults as values and secrets unmasked
InstancePlan.ports: DeclaredPort[] — host is what the allocator would choose, or null when it could find nothing

InstanceRow.primary: boolean — holds the pre-package network alias

InstanceSetting.key: string — as the manifest spells it, no SERVICE_<ID>_ prefix
InstanceSetting.kind: string — the manifest's type: string | secret | int | bool | enum | instanceRef
InstanceSetting.isDefault: bool — the value in force is the manifest's own default
InstanceSetting.defaultValue: string? — the manifest's own default, so the form can put it back; null for a secret, whose default is never handed out unasked
InstanceSetting.required: bool — instance_apply_settings refuses to empty one of these
InstanceSetting.options: string[] — an offer, not a constraint. For an instanceRef it is the installed instances answering the capability it names
InstanceSetting.label: Record<locale, string>

LogFile.label: string
LogFile.note: `id` is `<root>:<relative path>` — `app:` for files the code wrote under projects/<name>, `server:` for files the stack wrote under logs/projects/<name>. It is a handle, not a path: it is what app_log_open takes, and it is the reason no absolute path is ever accepted from the frontend. `modified` is epoch seconds so the date is formatted in the user's locale rather than the backend's.

MailBody.note: `headers`: every header flattened to one row per value, sorted by name; Mailpit serves them from a dedicated route, MailHog inlines them.

MailMessage.subject: string
MailMessage.note: `date` is passed through unparsed: the UI formats it in the user's locale, and the two servers disagree about which field it lives in, not about the format. `snippet` is null on MailHog, which does not send one — deriving it from the raw body would render MIME boundaries as preview text. `bcc` is populated only by Mailpit, which derives it from the SMTP envelope; MailHog cannot tell a Bcc from a To, so there it is empty rather than guessed. MailHog's `cc`/`replyTo` come from headers as one joined string per entry.

MailStatus.note: `unread` is null rather than 0 on MailHog, which has no concept of a read message — a zero would render as "all caught up" on a server that cannot know. `available` is false when the checkout has neither catcher at all, which is different from having one that is switched off.

MarketPackage.name: Record<locale, string>
MarketPackage.keywords: string[] — search terms the index publishes, so mysql is findable by typing 'database' and by typing 'mariadb'
MarketPackage.multiple: boolean — whether two versions may run at once

MarketStatus.fetched: boolean — false before the first refresh
MarketStatus.installed: number — version directories on this machine
MarketStatus.signed: boolean — whether signatures are being checked; false until a key is pinned
MarketStatus.signatureRequired: boolean — whether policy.market.requireSignature is set. Reported apart from `signed` because the pair is the story: required and not happening is a refusal, and it is the state a managed machine is in until ADR 0015's key exists.
MarketStatus.offlineBundle: string | null — the bundle policy.market.offlineBundle points at, which wins over the path the user chose. ADR 0011 makes this the only way an air-gapped machine ever gets a catalogue.
MarketStatus.constrained: boolean — whether a policy says anything about the market at all, so the page can explain a refusal before it happens

Migration.note: `version` is null when the tag does not state one — `latest`, `alpine` and `stable` yield nothing rather than a pin, because importing `latest` as a version invents a decision the source file deliberately did not make. Image matching is on the repository with registry and namespace stripped, so docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch and elasticsearch are one entry, and it is exact rather than fuzzy: a project running ghcr.io/acme/redis-shim is not running Redis, and guessing that it is enables a service nobody asked for. A registry port is not a tag — localhost:5000/mysql has no version. Two compose services mapping to one catalog id collapse to one, or the same .env key would be planned twice with different versions. `evidence` names what each conclusion was read from, for the same reason Detected carries it: a document root inferred wrongly produces a project that builds, starts and serves a 404.

MigrationPlan.note: `spec` is detection with the compose file layered on top, and the order is the point: detection reads the CODE and gets runtime, framework and document root; the compose file records what its author DECIDED — version, domain, extensions, services. Where both have an answer the compose file wins, because a guess loses to a declaration. `env` is the service enablement expressed as the same reviewed diff a preset import shows, rather than a second way of saying "turn these on".

MissingPackage.installable: boolean — whether the cached index offers it, which decides whether the UI can offer a button or only an explanation

PhpIniStatus.effectiveNote: What PHP in the RUNNING container reports right now, from one `docker exec php -r ini_get`. Null when nothing is running. Read rather than assumed because assuming was wrong: measured on a real stack, `php -i` says `Loaded Configuration File => (none)` — the official images ship no php.ini at all, so conf.d is not one layer among several but the only one — and `max_execution_time` is 0 under FPM, not the 30 the manual lists. The form uses these as placeholders, so it never shows a default the container does not have; it is also where an override is confirmed to have landed after a restart.
PhpIniStatus.note: `values` holds the four directives the form manages (memory_limit, upload_max_filesize, post_max_size, max_execution_time); `unmanaged` holds everything else the file contains, which is preserved verbatim on every write — the file is the user's and is safe to hand-edit and commit. `containerPath` is /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/zz-stackvo.ini: every PHP image the generator builds on (php:X-fpm, php:X-apache, php:X-cli for Swoole, and FrankenPHP, itself built on the official image) parses conf.d after its own php.ini, and `zz` sorts after the docker-php-ext-*.ini files the build writes, so what is set here is what PHP ends up with. Mounted read-only. `warning` is a legal but near-certainly-unintended combination — post_max_size below upload_max_filesize silently caps uploads at the smaller number, which is the classic "I raised the limit and it still fails".

PolicyMarket.constrained: boolean — whether the policy says anything about the market at all
PolicyMarket.registryUrl: string | null — a mirror the organisation runs; read by the network source (Faz 5)
PolicyMarket.offlineBundle: string | null — a directory to install from with no network. ADR 0011 makes this the only way an air-gapped machine gets a catalogue, so it is a first-class install path rather than an enterprise extra
PolicyMarket.requireSignature: boolean — the one key in the block that is a lock rather than a note: it can only turn verification ON, and there is no value of it that turns a check off (ADR 0009). Raises market::Trust to Signed, which refuses today because no key is pinned
PolicyMarket.allowedPackages: string[] — services that may be installed. EMPTY MEANS NO OPINION, not 'none'
PolicyMarket.allowedRegistries: string[] — registries an image may come from; a reference with no host counts as docker.io. Empty means no opinion
PolicyMarket.additionalKeys: number — how many extra signing keys were supplied, not which

Preflight.note: `detail` is what the machine said — a version, a path, the daemon's own error — and is deliberately not translated. `ready` ignores warnings: mkcert reports `warn` rather than `fail` because a stack without HTTPS still runs, it just serves a browser warning.

Preset.name: string?
Preset.note: `kind` and `version` are what make this a file format rather than "some JSON": `kind` is checked on load so a package.json is refused instead of read as an empty preset, and a `version` above what the app understands is refused rather than half-read — a newer preset may mean something different by a field this version already has, and applying the half we recognise writes a stack that matches neither machine. A service entry has exactly two fields; that is the mechanism by which no secret can be in one. `settings` is limited to DEFAULT_TLD_SUFFIX, SSL_ENABLE, DEFAULT_PHP_VERSION, DEFAULT_NODE_VERSION and DEFAULT_WEBSERVER, and the limit is re-checked on import — trusting the export side alone would let a hand-edited preset write any key it liked into somebody else's .env.

PresetPlan.name: string?
PresetPlan.note: `from` is null when the key is absent from .env entirely, which is different from present-and-empty. `unchanged` exists so "nothing to do" is distinguishable from "everything was rejected" — an empty `changes` list alone is ambiguous between the two, and they need opposite responses from the user. `kind` lets the UI group without parsing the key.

ProfileFile.note: `compressed` is read from the file's magic bytes. The overlay turns Xdebug's compression off, but a file written under somebody else's ini — or before profiling was turned on here — can still be gzipped, and the UI says so rather than the parser failing.

ProfileReport.creator: string
ProfileReport.note: `events` carries the units the file declares — do not assume microseconds. `summary` is the file's own total and is LARGER than `self_total`; the two are reported separately rather than conflated, and `percent` is a share of `self_total` so the column adds to 100. `functionCount` is how many distinct functions the file held before the top-60 cut. Measured on real output: 200,004 blocks aggregated to 5 functions, 10 MB parsed in under a second.

ProfilerStatus.traces: ProfileFile[] — read by profiler_flame, not profiler_read
ProfilerStatus.bytes: number — profiles AND traces; they share a directory and a disk
ProfilerStatus.note: Layered on XdebugStatus rather than duplicating it: the extension has to be compiled in for any mode, so `needsRebuild` and `active` mean exactly what they already meant. `mode` is one value and not a set because the three want different start triggers — stepping connects on the next request, profiling and tracing wait for a trigger so an idle stack does not fill a disk. `trace` is the third and closes F-3: it writes stacks, which is what a flame graph is built from, where a profile writes summed edges. The two lists are separate because they open different views. IMPLEMENTORS: xdebug.output_dir MUST exist before either mode records — Xdebug does not create it and writes nothing, silently, when it is missing.

ProgressEvent.subject: string
ProgressEvent.note: One line of a running process's merged stdout+stderr. Merged deliberately: docker compose writes progress to stderr and results to stdout, and separating them makes the log read out of order.

Project.name: string
Project.note: manifest_valid/manifest_errors are NEW: an invalid manifest must be visible in the list, not a silently missing project. generated_stale is measured from the manifest's mtime against the oldest of its generated outputs, NOT accumulated from `manifest:changed` events — the watcher cannot tell whose write it saw, so the app writing a manifest during project_create used to raise a 'needs regenerating' badge on a project it went on to generate half a second later. Derived, it is also right on first load, which an event-driven flag never was for an edit made while the app was closed.

ProjectLogFile.note: A LogFile with the project it belongs to. The id alone does not identify a file across the workspace — every Laravel project has an `app:storage/logs/laravel.log` — so the cross-project surface carries the pair, and app_log_open still takes them separately.

ProjectSpec.note: The create form's payload IS a project manifest. The old POST body used a flat shape (runtime, version, extensions at top level) that ProjectService then reassembled — and reassembled wrongly for node. v1 sends the manifest itself, so there is nothing to reassemble.

QuickCommand.note: `display` is the command as typed, so what runs and what is shown cannot drift. `interactive` decides where it goes — the user's terminal, or the operation console. `id` is the only thing quick_command_run accepts.

ReplRunner.note: `display` is the command as typed with the snippet left off, so what runs and what is shown cannot drift. `id` is the only thing repl_run accepts. `booted` is the difference between User::count() meaning something and meaning nothing.

ReplRun.note: Success is `exit_code == 0`, never "stderr is empty" — a PHP fatal goes to stdout. `limited` false means the in-container limit was not available, so the snippet may still be running in there after this app stopped waiting; the pane says so rather than letting a leak look like a clean stop. Streams are cut at 256 KiB from the FRONT, because a stack trace's useful half is its last lines.

ReplSnippet.note: The code, never the output — see repl_history.

ReleasePlan.note: `dockerfile` is shown before it is built — plan-then-apply, like the hosts file, the certificate and a preset import. A production image is the one artefact here that leaves the machine, so reviewing it is not optional politeness.

ReleaseResult.verification: { env_files: string[], xdebug_active: bool?, has_app: bool, clean: bool }
ReleaseResult.note: Read out of the BUILT image by running it, not inferred from the Dockerfile. `xdebugActive` is null for a node image — there is no PHP to ask, which is not the same as "no". `clean` is all three checks passing.

Service.id: string — the instance id (mysql-8-0) on the market model, the service id before it
Service.enabled: bool — whether it should run, which is not whether it is running
Service.built: bool — a container exists, running or not
Service.url: string? — the whole domain, suffix included
Service.health: string? — 'healthy' | 'unhealthy' | 'starting'; null when the image declares no healthcheck
Service.declaredPorts: DeclaredPort[] — every port the package declares, by handle, with the host number in force; empty before the migration
Service.aliases: string[] — the Docker network names this answers to, its own first; the second is the pre-package alias
Service.eolDate: string? — ISO date upstream support ends or ended
Service.companions: CompanionRow[] — containers shipped with this instance and not separately installable
Service.unmetDependencies: string[] — the subject of every required dependency that is unprovided or stopped

Bundled.versions: number — versions whose files were carried; lower than the index's total when something was withdrawn
Bundled.files: number — files written, index and package.json included
Bundled.bytes: number — their total size, so the person choosing a stick knows
Bundled.skipped: string[] — versions deliberately not carried, each with its reason. Empty is the normal case; a non-empty list is a fact the person carrying the bundle should read before they walk away from the network
Bundled.signed: boolean — whether registry.json.minisig travelled with it. A machine whose policy sets requireSignature refuses a bundle without one, and this is where that is cheap to find out

SourceProbe.location: string — exactly what was asked for
SourceProbe.resolved: string — where the bytes were actually fetched from; differs when a GitHub repository URL was translated
SourceProbe.currentSequence: number | null — the cached index's sequence, when there is one
SourceProbe.goesBackwards: boolean — this index is older than the one already here, which market_refresh refuses (T-6, replay)

Workspace.note: root is null when source is 'none'. `source` exists so the UI can say WHY it is pointing at a given checkout — silently guessing wrong would be worse than asking.

XdebugStatus.note: Three layers, deliberately not collapsed into one boolean. `enabled` is what the manifest asks for; `needsRebuild` is true while the image predates that ask, because extensions are compiled in and a toggle that looked done but changed nothing would be worse than no toggle; `active` is what the running container actually carries, and is null when there is no container to read. `hostPath` and `containerPath` are the two halves of the IDE's path mapping — the mapping is the step people get wrong, and both sides are already known here.

LocalOverride.note: B-2. `stackvo.local.json` is this machine's overrides for a committed manifest. `applied` is the dotted paths it currently supplies and `refused` the keys it may not carry (`name`, `runtime`) — both read back from the same merge the renderer runs, so the screen cannot disagree with what actually runs. `ignored` is git's own answer to whether the file would stay out of a commit, and is null when git had no answer: no git, or not a repository, which is not the same as “not ignored”.

HookPlan.digest: string? — what an approval would be recorded against; absent when the project has no host steps
HookPlan.note: B-3. A plan, not a result: it says what would run for one event and what would not, before anything is spawned — the same review-then-apply shape as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and a preset import. A refused step is NAMED here rather than silently skipped at run time, because “nothing happened and nothing said why” is indistinguishable from a hook that ran and did nothing.

HookStep.command: string — display only; nothing parses it back
HookStep.blocked: string? — policy-off | policy-host | needs-consent; absent means it runs

PackageReport.resealed: string[] — files whose hash the manifest had wrong
PackageReport.note: C-1. A manifest states the sha256 of every file the package ships and pkg::verify checks them on every read, so editing a compose fragment leaves a package that refuses to load with a message about bytes rather than about the line somebody just edited. That bookkeeping — not the JSON — is what made authoring a package impractical. `resealed` is what sealing changed (or would change, from a lint); `problems` is what it refused. A report with problems means NOTHING was written: sealing is bookkeeping, not a way past the validator.

DnsStatus.mechanism: string — resolver | network-manager | dnsmasq | systemd-resolved | nrpt | manual
DnsStatus.writable: bool — whether this app can apply the change itself, or only report it
DnsStatus.tld: string — the last label, which is what a resolver is pointed at
DnsStatus.tcp: bool — the second socket, reported separately because a port can be half-taken
DnsStatus.file: string? — the file this mechanism writes, where it has one
DnsStatus.configured: bool — whether this machine currently asks us for the suffix
DnsStatus.instruction: string — the file this app would write, or the line the user must place
DnsStatus.reload: string? — what is reloaded after the write, spelled out rather than done quietly
DnsStatus.foreign: string? — a file already at that path that is not ours, and what it says
DnsStatus.stale: string[] — resolver files this app wrote for a suffix the workspace has since left
DnsStatus.broken: bool — the machine asks us and nothing answers, which is the state where every name under the suffix fails
DnsStatus.note: E-1. The responder answers ONE suffix and refuses everything else — it never forwards, has no upstream and holds no cache, because an open forwarder on a machine is a thing that can be pointed at and a development tool has no business becoming the resolver for anything it did not create. `listening` is read from whether the socket is bound rather than from a preference: a setting saying yes over a port something else took would be a screen that lies. `mechanism` is detected rather than derived from the platform — on Linux WHICH file to write is a question about the machine (NetworkManager's dnsmasq, a standalone dnsmasq, systemd-resolved), and a guessed path is worse than no feature because it rearranges name resolution on a machine this app was wrong about. `manual` is the honest answer when none of them is found. `foreign` MUST be reported before the switch is pressed and the file MUST be copied aside rather than replaced — /etc/resolver/test is a path dnsmasq, Valet or a colleague's script may own, and taking a suffix away from another tool with no way back is not a thing to discover afterwards. `stale` exists because macOS's mechanism is one file PER SUFFIX: changing DEFAULT_TLD_SUFFIX leaves the old file pointing at a responder that now REFUSES that TLD, which is worse than never having written it — before, those names went upstream and failed honestly. `broken` is asked of the socket rather than of this process's own flag: a responder whose thread died and one in another copy of the app are both cases where the flag and the machine disagree, and the machine is right.

DnsCheck.name: string — the probe name, under the suffix and in no hosts file
DnsCheck.tcp: DnsProbe — asked the responder over TCP
DnsCheck.system: DnsProbe — asked this machine, the way a browser would
DnsCheck.public: DnsProbe — whether the rest of the internet still resolves
DnsCheck.ok: bool — udp and system together, which is the pair that means 'this works'
DnsCheck.note: Four probes rather than one verdict because the repair differs: a responder that does not answer is this app's fault, a machine that does not ask it is the resolver file's, and public names failing matters more than the feature does. `public` is informational on its own — an offline machine fails it — and is only ever decisive as a before/after comparison inside dns_resolver_install, which undoes its own change when public names stop resolving.

DnsProbe.detail: string — what came back, in words, for a screen that has to explain a failure

UserRoute.target: string — http:// or https://, origin only
UserRoute.rewrittenFrom: string? — what the user typed, when normalisation changed it
UserRoute.error: string? — set instead of `notes` when the route no longer normalises
UserRoute.note: E-4. Traefik routes every project and every catalogue service and nothing else, so a dev server somebody started by hand has no way in. The whole difficulty is one string: `http://localhost:3000` is read INSIDE Traefik's container, where localhost is Traefik — the config loads, the browser gets a 502, and nothing says why. So localhost and 127.0.0.1 are rewritten to host.docker.internal and the screen says so; refusing them would be defensible and useless, because it is the address people have. Checked on the way out rather than stored checked, so a route written today does not keep today's answer after the rule changes.

DbMovePlan.note: G-4. Dumping and restoring are two calls this app already had; what it did not have is an answer to “will this work”. Same engine is allowed. MySQL↔MariaDB is allowed WITH a warning — the same dump format in practice and genuinely different servers, and refusing it would refuse a thing that usually works. Crossing families is refused: a mysqldump file is not Postgres input and never becomes it, so accepting the request would empty the target and then fail on thousands of syntax errors. A downgrade is warned about because it is the direction that breaks quietly and does so partway through a restore that has already replaced the data.

DbMoved.bytes: number — the size of the dump that crossed, the only number that says anything actually moved

DbInstance.note: Separate from DbTarget rather than a field added to it: `db_targets` answers “which engines can this workspace dump”, one row per engine, and four callers read it that way. One row per instance would give all four a list twice as long for a question none of them asked. Stopped instances are included and marked — a list that hid one would leave somebody wondering where the instance they just created went.

PushPlan.registry: string? — the host the tag names
PushPlan.authenticated: bool? — whether this registry is in the user's Docker config; null means the answer could not be read, which is NOT “not logged in”
PushPlan.note: H-1. An image is pushed only after it has been verified: a registry keeps layers, deleting a tag does not remove what was in it, and on a shared registry somebody has already pulled it. A tag naming no registry is refused too — `docker push myapp:v1` goes to Docker Hub under whichever account is logged in. Credentials are not this app's business: `docker login` is the user's, exactly as ~/.ssh/config is.

IdleProject.seconds: number? — since the last request; absent when the log has never mentioned this router
IdleProject.note: I-2. Container CPU is not the signal and neither is the network counter: php-fpm sits near zero whether it is serving or asleep, and network moves for health checks and DNS — one mistake stops something in use, the other never stops anything. The honest answer is the proxy's, which wrote down when it last routed to each router. A project the log has NEVER mentioned is not suspendable: that is the state of a stack that just came up, and stopping everything the first time somebody enables this would be the worst possible introduction to it.

PerfLayer.enabled: bool — whether the setting says it lives in a volume
PerfLayer.exists: bool — whether that volume exists on the engine
PerfLayer.bytes: number? — what it holds, when the engine can say
PerfLayer.onHost: bool — whether the host still has a copy, which is what an editor indexes
PerfLayer.hostFiles: number? — files in the host copy, counted up to a cap
PerfLayer.note: I-1. Measured with examples/perf_layer_bench.rs on the machine this shipped from: vendor in a volume is 3.8x on a framework boot and does NOTHING for writes; storage/framework is what buys the writes, at 2.8x. That is why this is a list of directories rather than one 'make it fast' switch — the win depends on which directory moves, and a single switch would be a guess about somebody's project. NOT a synchronising layer: nothing on the host writes these directories, so nothing needs reconciling. A bidirectional sync (Mutagen's job) is deliberately not built here — see src-tauri/src/perf.rs for why a worse copy of it would be a liability rather than a feature.

Install.path: string — the installation root, or for Valet/Sail the directory that was pointed at
Install.sites: Array<{ name: string, path: string, domain: string | null, bytes: number, partial: boolean, detected: Detected, taken: boolean, services?: string[] }>
Install.note: L. `domain` is what the OTHER tool serves the site at, when the other tool says so: Laragon writes a vhost with a ServerName, Valet derives one from its own tld, and a Sail project's .env may carry an APP_URL. XAMPP and MAMP have nothing to read, so it is null and adoption asks. Sail's localhost defaults are treated as no domain rather than imported as one.

SiteSettings.env: Record<string,string> - set on the project's container, never written into the application's own .env
SiteSettings.directoryListing: bool - autoindex for nginx, file_server browse for Caddy
SiteSettings.sshAgent: bool - forward the host's SSH agent into the container
SiteSettings.listingSupported: bool - false for Apache and Swoole, which have no configuration file
SiteSettings.agentAvailable: bool - false when no agent is running on this machine
SiteSettings.server: string - named so the pane can say which server cannot list a directory
SiteSettings.note: M-10's socket is NOT $SSH_AUTH_SOCK. On macOS and Windows the daemon runs in a VM where the host's path means nothing, and Docker Desktop publishes the agent at /run/host-services/ssh-auth.sock instead; on Linux the daemon is the host and the real socket is the answer. Measured: a container with the Desktop path mounted answers 'ssh-add -l' with "The agent has no identities" - the agent replying - where an unforwarded one says it could not open a connection. Forwarding is off by default and per project, because anything in that container can sign with every key in the agent for as long as it is up.

Worktree.name: string — the project name, which is also the directory name, and the identity everything else keys off
Worktree.parent: string — the project it was branched from
Worktree.branch: string — the git branch checked out into it
Worktree.domain: string — a subdomain of the parent's, so it stays inside any wildcard route or certificate the parent has
Worktree.path: string — absolute, and recorded rather than derived: the project tree can be moved, and a derived path would send `git worktree remove` somewhere git has never heard of
Worktree.database: { instance: string, name: string, seededFrom?: string } | null
Worktree.env: Record<string,string> — what somebody typed. The database credentials are NOT here; they are derived from the instance on every render
Worktree.note: N. Stored in <root>/worktrees.json, outside every checkout, because the files in a worktree directory are the branch's and this app writes nothing there that git tracks. `seededFrom` is the only record of whether a branch started with a copy of the data or an empty schema, which is the question somebody asks three weeks later.

WorktreeRow.exists: bool — is the directory still there
WorktreeRow.dirty: bool | null — uncommitted work a removal would discard. null when git could not answer, which is a third state and not a warning
WorktreeRow.orphaned: bool — the record points somewhere git no longer has a checkout, usually because the folder was deleted by hand

WorktreePlan.newBranch: bool — whether the branch would be created rather than checked out
WorktreePlan.name: string
WorktreePlan.database: { instance: string, service: string, name: string, seed: bool, source?: string } | null
WorktreePlan.refused: string | null — one sentence naming why it cannot
WorktreePlan.note: Carries what it WOULD have produced even when refused: a dialog that blanks out on refusal makes the reason harder to act on, not easier.

WorktreeSupport.repository: bool — is the project's directory a git repository at all
WorktreeSupport.linked: bool — is it itself a linked worktree, as git sees it. Different from `record`, which means this app made it
WorktreeSupport.effectiveEnv: Record<string,string> | null — what this worktree's container is actually given, present only when `record` is. DB_PASSWORD is masked, and so is the same password inside DATABASE_URL
WorktreeSupport.domain: string | null — what a new worktree's hostname would be built under
WorktreeSupport.currentBranch: string | null — null for a detached head
WorktreeSupport.branches: Array<{ name: string, checkedOut: bool, current: bool }> — newest commit first
WorktreeSupport.instances: DbInstance[] — stopped ones included and marked
WorktreeSupport.reason: string | null — why worktrees are unavailable here
